name: Appointlet
tagline: Scheduling pages with availability, forms, payments, and team routing

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Up to 5 team members, 25 booked meetings/month and 1 scheduling page

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: Unlimited meetings/pages, reminders, manual confirmation, payments, pre-filled forms, redirects, Zapier/webhooks and removed branding
tiers.notes: Displayed prices imply 25% annual savings, although another official label says 20%; the actual $12/$9 card values are recorded.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom seats, security, implementation and support

pricing.freeTierCaps: 5 members, 25 booked meetings/month and 1 scheduling page
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; 14-day Premium trial that auto-downgrades to Free; seats are prorated
pricing.hiddenCosts: Premium is per member. The 30-day money-back guarantee applies only when there were zero bookings in the current billing cycle. Nonprofits and educational institutions can qualify for 25% off.

verdictSummary: The visible booking links loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Appointlet earns its keep through OAuth, calendar reliability, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a personal booking links tool that reads one calendar, publishes availability, reserves a slot, and writes the event back.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
whatYouLose: reliable reminders and timezone edge cases
calendar-provider edge cases and timezone correctness
whyPeopleStillPay: Appointlet: People pay because a booking tool must never double-book them, leak private events, or send the wrong time to a client.
ongoingBurden: Maintain OAuth, timezone data, webhooks, idempotency, reminders, calendar-provider quirks, and uptime.

priorArt.name: Cal.com
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source scheduling platform and OAuth reference.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Cal.com Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free plan does forms and payments for one person; round-robin and routing forms are paid.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Cal.diy
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The famous open-source answer, but the 2026 fork removed teams and workflows and is officially for hobbyist, non-production use.

rejectedAlternatives.name: YouCanBookMe Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free page handles forms and payments, but not the team routing Appointlet is hired for.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Appointlet is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Appointlet, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a personal booking links tool that reads one calendar, publishes availability, reserves a slot, and writes the event back.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: team routing and round robin; reliable reminders and timezone edge cases; calendar-provider edge cases and timezone correctness.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
